articles.title: Teacher held for TU paper leak within 5 minutes of exam commencement
articles.summary:
Just days after a leaked medical entrance examination paper in neighbouring India triggered nationwide protests and forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign, a similar breach has emerged at Nepal’s largest university.

The question paper for Tribhuvan University’s Master of Business Studies (MBS) first-semester examination was leaked on July 24, the same day Pradhan stepped down in India. The incident came to light on July 25, after evidence showed that the paper had been circulating online while the examination was underway.

The paper was circulated in a WhatsApp group just five minutes after the examination began, exposing serious lapses in the security and confidentiality mechanisms surrounding university examinations. The incident has raised fresh questions about the integrity of Tribhuvan University’s examination system, which has faced repeated controversies over the years.

Police have arrested a teacher in connection with the leak.

The Cyber Bureau of Nepal Police arrested Sandip Singh, better known among students as “Sulab Sir”, on charges of circulating the question paper as the examination had just begun. Investigators said Singh teaches at Himalaya College, Koteshwar and the KMC College, Bagbazar.

According to Senior Superintendent Anupam Shumsher Rana, spokesperson for the Central Investigation Bureau (CIB), police arrested Singh from Bhaktapur and launched an investigation against him for allegedly violating examination confidentiality provisions under the Education Act, 1971.

During questioning, Singh claimed that he had only forwarded a question paper sent to him by an unidentified person to a WhatsApp group named “MBS First Semester Section C”. Investigators said they have found no evidence so far that he received any financial benefit from the leak.

The breach came to light after a student in the group took screenshots of the exchange and shared them with a popular Facebook page, prompting the Ministry of Education to intervene.

After his involvement became public, Singh posted a message in the WhatsApp group, which had 1,023 members and carried the description “Let’s help each other”.

“Thank you, all my dear students,” he wrote.

He later sought to defend his actions, saying: “Sometimes, things like this happen in life. I have always tried to help from the bottom of my heart, and now I need your help. I merely forwarded a paper that was already circulating on social media and other WhatsApp groups. I was just at home, looking at my mobile phone.”

Screenshots obtained by Kantipur show an individual saved as “Sulab Sir” sharing a PDF file of the MBS question paper five minutes after the examination began on July 24.

Shortly afterwards, a student identified as “Keshav Bhatt” asked, “Sir, please send the solution as well.”

Singh replied, “Okay,” and later shared a 16-page handwritten solution to the examination questions.

The WhatsApp conversation also showed students discussing examination arrangements while the test was still underway.

One student asked whether candidates were allowed to enter the examination hall 30 minutes late and requested responses from anyone who had experienced the situation. Another student replied that it depended on the examination centre.

Another student, apparently referring to the upcoming Economics paper, requested that the questions also be uploaded on the group.

“I might have to go late for Eco [Economics] now, Sir. Please upload the questions like this,” the student wrote.

“I will provide Eco as well, please study well,” Singh responded.

At the time of the exchange, at least 35 members were visible as active in the group. Another student described it as the “best group” for working professionals.

During the investigation, police detained several other individuals along with Singh. However, they were later released after investigators said there was insufficient evidence to proceed against them.

Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel said the ministry coordinated with the Ministry of Home Affairs after receiving information about the leak on Saturday and instructed Inspector General of Police Dan Bahadur Karki to expedite the investigation.

“We forwarded the screenshots of the messages to the Cyber Bureau, and two individuals were arrested on Sunday morning,” Pokharel told journalists at the ministry. “The police are conducting further investigations, and they will provide detailed information.”

Pokharel said preliminary findings indicated that the leak was carried out by a teacher rather than a Tribhuvan University employee.

Following the leak, Tribhuvan University’s Faculty of Management formed a probe committee on Sunday to investigate the breach.

The committee, led by Prof Dr Achyut Gyawali, includes Pushkar Raikhala, deputy director of the Monitoring Directorate, and Mahesh Raj Ojha, a member of the Central Examination Steering Committee.

The Examination Control Division said the panel would determine whether the paper was leaked, how the breach occurred, who was responsible, and recommend legal action.

Education experts say the latest leak reflects deeper structural flaws in Nepal’s examination system, where weak oversight, commercial pressures and political interference have allowed such breaches to recur.

Educationist Binay Kumar Kusiyait said repeated question paper leaks were a consequence of the growing commercialisation of the education sector.

“These kinds of issues started surfacing over the last 15 to 20 years. The primary focus of educational institutions has shifted from producing quality students to finding ways to commercialise education and artificially inflate results. This is the root of the problem,” Kusiyait told Kantipur.

“When the focus shifts entirely to the quality of results rather than the quality of students, unethical practices are bound to happen. The drive to earn more money by spending money naturally leads to this.”

Kusiyait also criticised Tribhuvan University’s failure to strengthen monitoring mechanisms and improve its question paper distribution system.

“In many instances, action could not be taken due to political patronage and protection. That is precisely why these incidents keep repeating,” he said.

The leak has also triggered strong criticism from student organisations, with the Free Student Union (FSU) at Tribhuvan University demanding accountability from university officials.

The union has called for the resignation of Mahananda Chalise, dean at the Faculty of Management, and Bharat Rai, assistant dean in charge of examinations.

In a statement on Sunday, FSU president Deepak Raj Joshi demanded an impartial investigation within two days and the publication of its findings. He sought clarity on how the question paper was leaked and who was involved, while calling for strict legal action against those responsible.

Joshi said the leak of a question paper while an examination was underway had raised serious concerns about the confidentiality, fairness and credibility of the examination system.

Any act that undermines students’ hard work, public trust and the university’s reputation was unacceptable, he said.

The latest breach is not an isolated incident. The country witnessed repeated cases of examination papers being compromised, from Grade 12 board examinations to university and medical entrance tests, over the past decade and a half.

Earlier this year, on May 12, the Cyber Bureau arrested two people after question papers for Grade 12 Management and Science examinations conducted by the National Examination Board were leaked before the exams.

The bureau arrested 37-year-old Nirajan Shahi, a counselling officer at a local college, and 30-year-old IT officer Prem Kumar Shrestha. Investigators said Shrestha, who was responsible for printing the question papers, handed them over to Shahi shortly before the examination.

Police officials said, however, that this was the first time the bureau had investigated a question paper leak directly linked to Tribhuvan University.

One of the most prominent examination scandals occurred in December 2014, when the MBBS entrance examination was cancelled after its question paper was leaked.

The Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) raided a college in Battisputali, Kathmandu and arrested two people after they were found with the Biology question paper for the examination scheduled for 1:00 pm that day.

After a lengthy legal process, the Special Court convicted Prabhat Kumar Kushwaha, identified as the mastermind behind the leak, sentencing him to four years in prison and imposing a fine of Rs3.4 million.

His accomplices, Dharmendra Yadav and Diwas Yadav, were each sentenced to one year in prison and fined Rs900,000 and Rs500,000 respectively. Maheshwar Prasad Yadav received a two-year prison sentence and a fine of Rs1.7 million.

The court also sentenced the college director Devi Ram Pandey to nine months in prison and fined him Rs505,000. College teacher Khetarnath Sapkota was sentenced to one month and 15 days in prison and fined Rs2,500.

articles.title: What makes food sold in most Nepali stores ‘organic’? The label
articles.summary:
For urban residents navigating Kathmandu’s grocery stores, regional delicacies from specific districts carry an almost magical appeal. Beans from Jumla, cliff-bee honey from Surkhet, ginger from Salyan, apples and potato from Mustang evoke pictures of pristine mountain soil. Yet behind the idyllic images printed on slick packaging lies a stark reality—much of what is sold with the labelled ‘organic’, ‘pure’, or ‘100 percent natural’ is nothing more than unverified marketing hype.

Consumer rights activists and agricultural experts have long warned that the city’s appetite for indigenous foods has spawned a lucrative grey market. Urban shoppers willingly pay premium prices for items labelled with revered geographic identities—such as Pokhara’s Jethobudho rice, Jumla’s Simi and Marsi rice, Khopasi’s khuwa, Ilam’s tea, Gulmi’s coffee, or Mudhe’s potatoes—without any guarantee of their origin or chemical purity.

“City dwellers searching for organic and native flavours are ready to empty their pockets without a second thought, lured by beautiful labels and charming product names,” said Bhupendra Nirajan, general manager and food inspector at NEPCERT, one of Nepal's accredited organic certification bodies. “The uncomfortable truth today is that neither the seller nor the consumer can verify whether these goods actually come from the soil of those remote villages.”

According to Nirajan, consumers have developed a habit of trusting the tag on a package rather than demanding proof of the product’s actual quality.

The systemic disparity between actual agricultural output and market availability was underscored on Friday by Ram Bhakta Adhikari, acting chief of the Agriculture Development Office in Jumla.

“Jumla produces approximately 3,600 tonnes of beans annually, out of which only around 55 tonnes are exported outside the district,” said Adhikari. “Yet in Kathmandu’s supermarkets, online stores, and vegetable outlets, so-called ‘Jumla beans’ are sold in massive quantities all year round.”

This glaring discrepancy points to widespread mislabelling across the supply chain, where produce grown in low-altitude districts using fertilisers is routinely packaged and passed off under high-value mountain brands.

“It astounds us as well. Most of the beans harvested in Jumla are consumed locally. While our beans are renowned for their distinct taste and quality, produce from entirely different districts is clearly being passed off under Jumla's name in Kathmandu,” said Adhikari.

This regulatory vacuum is hardly a new phenomenon in the country’s food market. Various studies show how toxic pesticide residues routinely exceed permissible levels in produce entering urban centres from major farming belts. Despite periodic public outcry over chemical contamination, state mechanisms have consistently failed to implement integrated tracking systems, leaving city markets vulnerable to fraudulent labelling practices.

The Department of Food Technology and Quality Control (DFTQC), the primary state entity responsible for enforcing food safety, has urged consumers not to rely solely on labels when purchasing food items sold as ‘organic’ in the market. The department stated that consumers must check whether products claiming to be organic possess valid certification, warning that traders making false claims will face legal action under existing laws.

The department acknowledges the pervasive nature of false labelling but places the burden of proof partly on buyers. “Writing ‘organic’ on a label does not make a product organic,” said Bal Kumari Sharma, spokesperson and senior food research officer at the DFTQC. “For a product to be legally sold as organic, it must undergo formal certification from an authorised body and display an official certified logo on its packaging.”

Sharma clarified that the government itself does not directly issue organic certificates to individual farmers. Instead, certification is handled by registered private agencies supervised by the Department of Agriculture.

“During market inspections, if our officers encounter products labelled as organic, we immediately demand legal certification,” said Sharma. “If a business labels its goods as organic without valid paperwork, it constitutes consumer deception and is subject to prosecution under existing food safety and consumer protection laws.”

While existing legal provisions lack a dedicated standalone clause defining the word 'organic', authorities rely on general provisions against misleading labelling and consumer fraud to penalise offenders.

“Our primary mandate is to monitor quality, safety, and label compliance,” said Sharma. “We inspect samples, verify certification for special claims like organic or halal (Arabic word meaning permissible), and act upon public complaints. Consumers must not rely blindly on claims printed on a bag; they must check for official logos and report suspicious products directly to us.”

Nepal’s legal framework for organic farming is anchored in the Guidelines for Group Certification Internal Control System of Organic Agriculture Production 2012 formulated by the Ministry of Agriculture Development. The guidelines set the regulatory protocol for certifying organic produce, processed foods, and agricultural exports.

At present, only eight private agencies are officially registered with the government to provide organic certification services in accordance with national and international standards. These include Organic Certification Nepal, NEPCERT, Sakura Herbs and Agro Pvt Ltd, Certification of Environmental Standards Nepal Pvt Ltd, Himalayan Certification Nepal, Nepal Organic Certification International Surkhet, IMO Kathmandu, and Environment Food and Agriculture Certification Pvt Ltd.

However, industry insiders argue that the monitoring framework exists largely on paper. Yam Kumari Shrestha, senior horticulture development officer at the Division of Agricultural Productivity under the Department of Agriculture, noted that state oversight is mostly confined to administrative check-ins.

“We monitor these agencies during their annual registration renewals and maintain records of the products they certify,” said Shrestha. “Certification activities dropped noticeably following the Covid-19 pandemic. Currently, tea and coffee make up the vast majority of certified organic goods because they are primary export commodities bound for international markets. Herbs, timur (Sichuan pepper), ginger and vegetables follow.”

Shrestha revealed that certified organic livestock and dairy products remain virtually non-existent in Nepal. “There is no organic certification for eggs or meat in the country. Within the dairy sector, only a single variety of cheese produced by the Dairy Development Corporation holds organic certification. Cardamom was certified once years ago, but that status has since lapsed.”

A severe bottleneck in the state’s enforcement capability is the complete absence of an integrated government laboratory equipped to verify organic authenticity or perform specialised chemical analyses. Neither the Department of Agriculture nor the accredited private certification agencies possess state-of-the-art testing facilities. Consequently, agencies must outsource sample testing to private laboratories, which charge exorbitant rates.

According to food inspectors, conducting even a basic laboratory test can cost anywhere between Rs15,000 and Rs16,000. “When combined with official audit fees, the total cost for obtaining an organic certificate ranges from Rs60,000 to Rs150,000, as confirmed by certification directors,” said Bhola Shrestha, director of Organic Certification Nepal.

For Nepal’s smallholder farmers—who form the backbone of the rural economy—these prohibitive costs create an insurmountable barrier. Bhola Shrestha confirmed that certification fees remain well out of reach for average producers.

Furthermore, the rigorous bureaucratic procedures demand meticulously updated farm diaries, paper logs of every seed and fertiliser source, strictly maintained soil buffer zones, and specialised transport protocol.

“For small farmers working two or four katthas of land, individual certification is financially impossible,” said Nirajan. “Even when farmers form cooperatives to share costs, they face immense risk. Under strict organic standards, if just one out of a hundred farmers in a group secretly uses chemical fertiliser or pesticide, the entire group’s organic certificate is instantly revoked.”

Compounding these structural hurdles is the total lack of financial guarantees. Farmers who invest time and capital to secure genuine organic certification are rarely offered a guaranteed premium price by middle-tier traders or urban retail chains. Deprived of technical support from local governments and facing uncertain market returns, smallholders naturally abandon formal certification altogether—leaving the market wide open for unverified, falsely labelled goods to flourish across the country.

articles.title: The journey for fodder is too often becoming a final one
articles.summary:
Seventeen-year-old Dammara Dhami had set out to do what countless women and girls in rural Nepal do every day: collect grass for livestock. A week ago, that routine chore turned fatal.

Dhami, from ward 2 of Malera in Bungal Municipality of Bajhang district, tripped while cutting grass on a steep cliff and fell around 300 metres to her death.

In Bungal, her death is far from an isolated tragedy. Every year, four or five people in the municipality lose their lives in similar accidents.

“Every village here has families who have lost loved ones to these cliffs,” said Nirajan Kunwar, ward 5 chair of the municipality. “People cannot survive without raising livestock, and to feed them they have to climb dangerous cliffs. A single misstep can cost a life.”

According to Kunwar, 22 people have died in cliff-related accidents in Bungal over the past five years alone.

The tragedy is repeated across Nepal’s hills. From Sudurpaschim province in the west to Koshi province in the east, fatal falls while collecting fodder and firewood have become a grim but familiar part of rural life.

Behind almost every such death lies the same combination of poverty, rugged geography and an agrarian economy heavily dependent on livestock. Cattle and buffaloes provide milk, manure and an important source of household income, but keeping them alive often requires villagers to climb dangerous cliffs every day in search of fodder.

The burden falls disproportionately on women.

In many rural communities, collecting fodder and firewood remains largely women’s work. Every day they negotiate narrow foot trails, scale steep cliffs and carry heavy loads of grass home, often without any form of safety equipment or secure access.

Local representatives say the deaths will continue unless safer fodder sources, improved livestock management, better access trails and other practical interventions are introduced.

Some families have endured the same tragedy repeatedly.

In March 2021, 19-year-old Dammara Bohara of Bhannegada in ward 1 of Bitthadchir Rural Municipality died after falling off a cliff while cutting grass, leaving behind her two-year-old son and husband Harish Bohara.

It was the third such death in Harish’s family.

Harish's mother, Ratna Devi, died at the cliff in 2003 while collecting fodder. In 2014, Devi Bohara, another member of the family, also fell to her death there.

Haris was only 11 when his mother died. Today, after losing his wife, he is raising their seven-year-old son alone.

According to Janaki Bohara, former vice-chair of Bitthadchir Rural Municipality, at least 19 people from Bitthadchir and neighbouring Chaukham in Baitadi district have died after falling from the same cliff and surrounding areas over the past five years.

The Panakot cliff near the district headquarters of Chainpur has acquired a similarly deadly reputation.

“I have lived here since my marriage 25 years ago,” said Parbati Oli of Jayaprithvi Municipality. “Over these years, the Panakot cliff has claimed 27 lives. One or two people die almost every year. But we have no choice. If we don’t cut grass, we cannot keep cattle.”

Unlike the plains, where fodder can be cultivated more easily, settlements across Nepal’s mid-hills are scattered over rugged terrain. Forests and grasslands are often located above or below sheer cliffs, forcing villagers to negotiate hazardous slopes every day.

The danger intensifies during the monsoon, when rain makes rocks slippery and loose soil unstable. Yet despite decades of fatal accidents, few systematic measures have been introduced to reduce the risks. Many settlements still lack safe access trails, rope support systems or community fodder plantations that could reduce the need to climb dangerous cliffs.

The stories from Bajhang are echoed across the country.

In Achham, 50-year-old Dhani Budha died in December 2025 after slipping while cutting grass at Maleghadi Mela in ward 1 of Mellekh Rural Municipality. Earlier, in June 2023, 62-year-old Parudevi Budha of ward 5 of Ramaroshan Rural Municipality was killed after falling from the Sindure cliff while collecting fodder.

“We are forced to go to terrifying cliffs just to keep our kitchen fires burning,” said Parudevi’s sister-in-law, Mansara Budha. “If we don’t go, what will we feed our cattle? Our very existence depends on these cliffs.”

Similar tragedies occur every year across Karnali province.

In July 2023, Dhanamaya Khatri of ward 7 of Bafikot Rural Municipality in Rukum West died after a landslide buried her while she was cutting grass.

Official records suggest the true scale of the problem may be even greater than reported.

According to the District Police Office in Bajhang, nine people have died after falling from cliffs over the past three years. Information Officer Deepak Bista said many families perform cremations without notifying the police about deaths.

Police in Achham recorded five similar deaths during the same period.

Deputy Superintendent of Police Om Prakash Khanal, chief of the District Police Office, Achham, said the district’s rugged terrain and remoteness often make timely rescue operations impossible.

“By the time information reaches us, it is often too late,” he said.

Local officials say geography alone does not explain the high death toll.

“In rural hill communities, women are primarily responsible for collecting grass, firewood, bedding for livestock and fuel,” said Ambika Chalaune, mayor of Panchadewal Binayak Municipality. “That is why they are disproportionately exposed to these risks.”

Data from the Karnali Province Police Office show that 522 people have died after falling from cliffs over the past 12 years. The highest annual toll was recorded in the 2023-24 fiscal year, when 64 people died. In the last fiscal year (2025-26), another 33 people died in similar incidents.

Deputy Inspector General Jayaraj Sapkota, chief of the Karnali Province Police Office, said most victims die while collecting fodder or firewood. However, he said police have recently recorded fatal falls involving people distracted by mobile phones while carrying heavy loads across steep terrain.

The problem extends well beyond Karnali.

In Lumbini province, 107 people died last fiscal year after falling from cliffs, trees or wells, according to provincial police records. Palpa recorded the highest number of fatalities, with 25 deaths.

Provincial police data show that 16 people died in Pyuthan, 14 in Dang, 13 in Rolpa, 12 in Gulmi, six each in Rukum East and Rupandehi, and five each in Bardiya and Arghakhanchi.

Baburam Karki, president of the Nepal Red Cross Society, Palpa, said difficult terrain is only one factor behind the accidents.

“Poor physical condition, mental stress, anxiety or even a brief lapse in concentration while climbing trees or cliffs can prove fatal,” he said.

Koshi province presents an equally alarming picture.

Provincial police recorded 1,016 deaths from falls off cliffs and unsafe trails over the past five fiscal years. Of them, 779 were men and 237 were women.

The annual death toll stood at 224 in 2021-22; 200 in 2022-23; 210 in 2023-24; 189 in 2024-25; and 193 in 2025-26.

Senior Superintendent of Police Yogendra Singh Thapa, spokesperson for the Koshi provincial police, said the pattern differs by gender.

“Women are more likely to be involved in accidents while collecting grass and firewood, whereas men are more frequently injured or killed while grazing livestock or walking along remote trails,” he said.

Fatal falls are not confined to the remote western hills.

Even in Makawanpur, which borders the Kathmandu Valley, police recorded 16 deaths, including 10 women, from cliff falls during the last fiscal year.

On Friday, 45-year-old Ishwar Thing from ward 9 of Kailash Rural Municipality died after falling while cutting grass in a hill forest about 500 metres from his home.

Last December, 48-year-old Sitamaya Ghalan of ward 6 Raksirang Rural Municipality also died after falling off a hill in the Silinge Community Forest.

Local governments say the deaths are not isolated mishaps but the result of decades of neglect.

“There is no tradition of planting fodder trees on private farmland,” said Dev Krishna Pudasaini, chair of Indrasarowar Rural Municipality. “As a result, people are forced to venture to dangerous cliffs in search of fodder.”

Rajkumar Malla, chair of Raksirang Rural Municipality, said the danger extends beyond fodder collection.

“Even walking along narrow, slippery foot trails to reach local markets can be deadly,” he said. “Three women died in our municipality last fiscal year after falling from such trails.”

articles.title: Q&A: Generating Rs29.32 billion from power exports is a remarkable national milestone
articles.summary:
For a country aiming for ambitious energy targets, Nepal’s private power producers find themselves navigating a maze of regulatory halts and a massive gridlock. The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) currently faces a backlog of unsigned Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) totalling nearly 16,000 megawatts, leaving project developers in uncertainty. While the government previously introduced a policy framework to generate 15,000 MW, rapid exhaustion of designated quotas led to a prolonged suspension of standard PPAs since 2018/19. As developers call for policy consistency and open market access to allow private sector power trading, the urgency to address these systemic bottlenecks has never been higher.

The Post’s Biken K Dawadi and Seema Tamang sat down with Mohan Kumar Dangi, the newly elected President of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), to dissect the structural causes behind the PPA backlog, the necessity of power trading rights for private developers, and the strategic roadmaps required to transform Nepal’s energy sector from quota-driven constraints into a fully realised necessity.

Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has a backlog of several unsigned Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), totalling around 16,000 MW. How does the IPPAN plan to break this gridlock?

Let us look at the background first. Back in 2015/16, the Government of Nepal introduced a policy to develop 15,000 MW of power. That 15,000 MW target was categorised into three primary types: Run-of-River (RoR), Storage/Reservoir, and Peaking Run-of-River (PRoR), alongside a 10 percent quota dedicated to solar energy to achieve an optimal energy mix concept that would make our nation self-reliant. Under that target, a quota of 5,250 MW was designated specifically for RoR projects.

That 5,250 MW quota for RoR projects was exhausted very quickly. Consequently, from 2018/19 onwards, standard RoR PPAs were suspended. Later, during the tenure of former minister Rajendra Lingden, 1,500 MW was transferred from the unused reservoir quota to the RoR quota because not a single reservoir-type PPA had taken place, whereas PRoR PPAs were continuing. That brought total RoR PPAs to 6,750 MW.

The point I am emphasising is that this issue is not something that just happened yesterday. Standard RoR PPAs have been largely halted since 2018/19. The PRoR quota has now been exhausted as well. The storage quota remains unfulfilled because storage projects haven’t been initiated. The government did bring forward positive measures for reservoir projects in the recent budget—such as extending licenses to 50 years and permitting developers to collect 40 percent equity from the public after financial closure.

Currently, projects generating around 16,140 MW have completed their feasibility studies, and many have obtained or applied for generation licenses. They are all lined up waiting for PPAs. The government previously pledged in its 100-point action plan that PPAs would be executed within 180 days. We have placed our trust in the government’s official announcements. Over 100 days have elapsed out of those 180 days, and we expect a breakthrough soon.

So, effectively, since 2018/19, barring that 1,500 MW transferred quota in 2022/23, there have been no regular PPAs?

Exactly. That 1,500 MW PPA was done purely by shifting allocations from the reservoir pool. It cannot be considered part of a regular, continuous process. Therefore, standard PPAs have remained stalled since 2018/19.

And Peaking (PRoR) PPAs are not moving forward either?

The peaking quota of 2,800 MW has also been filled. So, PPA processing across these categories is virtually at a standstill right now. While the reservoir category remains open, there are few viable private reservoir projects ready, rendering the overall situation stagnant.

Last year’s budget introduced a ‘take-and-pay’ provision. Previously, through IPPAN’s initiatives, former leadership at NEA had agreed that projects up to 10 MW would not have to wait in a queue for PPAs. But with the introduction of the take-and-pay provision, even those small-scale projects came to a halt.

Many private developers are deeply concerned about these conditions. How is IPPAN engaging with the government to protect investor capital?

First of all, ‘take-and-pay’ cannot be considered a real Power Purchase Agreement. It is not bankable. Financial institutions will not extend loans under a take-and-pay clause, making such agreements practically useless.

Regarding capital protection, private developers did not take survey and generation licenses on a whim. The Government of Nepal opened these opportunities. The Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, alongside the Department of Electricity Development, issues licenses to us. It is unjustified for the state utility, NEA, which falls under the same ministry, to say it will not execute PPAs.

We recognise the operational challenges. Currently, around 4,300 MW is operational in Nepal’s total system, and roughly 6,200 MW of projects are under construction. Managing all this capacity is challenging for NEA alone. That is precisely why we advocate issuing power trading licenses and transmission construction licenses to the private sector.

If we strictly insisted on our constitutional rights without offering solutions, our single demand would simply be: “Sign our PPAs regardless.” But we observe that the NEA is struggling to manage energy absorption, explore export markets, and expand domestic demand. Look at the domestic market potential—we import LPG gas worth Rs60 billion annually. If we replaced LPG with electric cooking, or expanded electric vehicle infrastructure, domestic consumption would surge.

Since state mechanisms have not fully capitalised on these areas, opening up power trading and transmission to the private sector is a constructive solution. If the government issues licenses, collects taxes, and regulates under existing law, refusing to sign PPAs afterwards is untenable.

Despite these challenges, Nepal achieved nearly Rs29.32 billion in revenue from power export. In light of this milestone, how do you view IPPAN’s push for private cross-border power trade?

Generating Rs29.32 billion from power exports is a remarkable national milestone. It underscores the vast economic potential of Nepal's energy sector. However, we must recognise that this record revenue was built on the foundation of private sector investments. Over 80 percent of the operational capacity generating that exported energy was constructed by private power producers.

Our demand for internal and cross-border power trading licenses is supported by this proven track record over the past twenty-five years.

The Electricity Act was promulgated in 1992, followed by the Electricity Regulations in 1993. By 1998, standard PPA tariffs were established, facilitating private sector entry. In 1998, Nepal’s total installed capacity was merely 252 MW. Today, total capacity stands at roughly 4,300 MW, with over 3,500 MW built directly by private power producers. State-owned generation accounts for only about 800 MW. This proves that the private sector possesses the technical and financial capacity to execute large-scale infrastructure.

Second, private developers have built hundreds of kilometres of transmission lines to connect their power stations to NEA substations across multiple voltage thresholds—33 kV, 66 kV, 132 kV, and 220 kV.

Consider a recent example: the 220 kV Markhu-Chok to Bharatpur line. The NEA had awarded that major transmission corridor to a Chinese contractor eight to ten years ago, but the project stalled due to low bidding, local disputes, and cost overruns. Private developers stepped in, took over the project, injected the shortfall capital, and completed the line within six to seven months. This demonstrates our ability to construct transmission corridors efficiently.

Third, look at regional dynamics. India’s installed capacity stands at nearly 600,000 MW, with private enterprises accounting for approximately 49 percent. Major private corporations like Tata Power, Adani Power, and Torrent Power handle thousands of megawatts seamlessly under clear statutory guidelines for open access, wheeling, and private power trading.

Following your recent interaction with the Indian Ambassador, what progress or resistance are you seeing regarding private power trade?

Our primary market is India. Bangladesh represents a secondary market, while China currently shows limited interest in power imports from Nepal. In India, private companies trade freely without governmental bottlenecks. Why should Nepal rely solely on Government-to-Government (G2G) mechanisms when Business-to-Business (B2B) trade can be far more flexible and responsive?

Even with the record-high export numbers achieved by the state utility, imagine how much higher those figures could be if private entities were granted trading licenses. Trading power is not a luxury for us. It is an urgent necessity. Developers have effectively become farmers who grow perishable crops but are barred from selling them while their produce goes to waste. Seven or eight private applications for trading licenses have been sitting at the Ministry for six to seven years without action.

Officials often point to the Electricity Act of 1992 (2049 BS) as a legal hurdle for granting private trading licenses. What is your position on this legal argument?

I disagree with that interpretation. A subsidiary company established under NEA—which is registered as a limited company just like our private companies—was granted a power trading license three to four years ago. That entity has held a license without conducting significant trade, while private developers who are ready to trade are denied licenses under the pretext of the law.

The law cannot treat one corporate entity differently from another simply based on state ownership. If the existing framework allows a state-owned subsidiary to trade, it permits private corporate entities to trade as well.

When late Minister Shailaja Acharya fixed PPA rates in 1998, critics doubted whether the private sector could build power projects. Had the government not trusted the private sector back then, total national capacity today would remain around 800 MW—the exact capacity built directly by the state—and the country would still be facing 18 hours of daily load-shedding. Today, the private sector supplies over 3,500 MW.

Obtaining a trading license does not mean trading begins overnight. Setting up international trade desks, strategic partnerships, wheeling arrangements, and commercial agreements takes four to five years. Power development and trading require long-term planning.

Under the 25-year agreement between Nepal and India, Nepal aims to export 10,000 MW of electricity to India over the next decade. Is this target realistic from IPPAN’s standpoint?

It is achievable. Following joint steering committee meetings, Nepal’s approved export capacity to India reached 1,650 MW. We have nine years remaining to scale up production and export the remaining 8,400 MW. Indian investments, such as the Arun III project, are actively underway. The government has set a broader target of generating 30,000 MW within ten years.

During our executive committee’s recent meeting with the Indian Ambassador, the Ambassador expressed keen interest in ensuring this 10,000 MW target is realised efficiently. When power is generated and exported, the broader economy benefits. Private hydro construction directly sustains domestic industries like steel, cement, transport and local employment.

Nepal recently reached an agreement to export 40 MW to Bangladesh via the Indian grid. How do you view the prospects there?

Bangladesh is an attractive market with high demand, and tariff rates offered there are competitive. However, cross-border transmission to Bangladesh requires transit through Indian territory, making India’s cooperation essential. That involves diplomatic channels beyond the direct scope of private developers.

Some commentators argue that Nepal should retain all generated electricity domestically rather than exporting it. Domestic utilisation is indeed the top priority because local consumption yields high economic multipliers. However, when surplus power is generated during the monsoon, and domestic demand cannot immediately absorb it, exporting that excess energy prevents financial losses for both developers and the state.

Beyond PPAs and power trading, project financing, climate risks, and disaster insurance remain major challenges for developers. How is IPPAN addressing these issues?

Liquidity in the banking system fluctuates. To secure long-term capital, we are encouraging alternative financial tools such as green bonds, specialised mutual funds, and climate finance structures. Hydropower yields predictable, long-term cash flows backed by fixed PPA tariffs, making it a suitable candidate for these instruments.

On insurance and natural disaster risks, recent floods demonstrated the vulnerability of headworks and powerhouses located near riverbeds. IPPAN is working to establish tailored insurance mechanisms specifically for the energy sector. We are advocating for policy guidelines that prevent a single insurance company from taking on excessive risk concentration within a single river basin. Distributing policies across multiple underwriters ensures structural stability for both the insurance industry and energy developers. Furthermore, engineering designs must adapt to rising climate risks by incorporating higher safety margins and headframe elevations.

What is your unifying vision for IPPAN during your tenure?

IPPAN was established in 2001 and has grown over the past two decades into a vital national institution representing around 700 member companies. Having worked closely with the last three leaderships, I have observed internal debates during leadership transitions. Healthy debate and democratic competition within an active organisation are positive forces.

Once elections conclude, internal differences end. My goal is to lead a fully unified IPPAN. Our main priority remains clear: Securing investment safety, ensuring policy certainty, breaking the PPA gridlock, and opening private power trading and transmission lines for the sustainable growth of Nepal’s energy sector.

articles.title: Having a camera and a mic doesn’t make you a journalist
articles.summary:
The way we practise journalism has changed over time with technological advances. Today’s journalists are expected not only to handle a camera and microphone but also to be multimedia-savvy and to develop digital storytelling skills. However, not everyone with a camera and a mic practises journalism ethically. Some self-styled journalists film solely for views on social media such as Facebook and YouTube. In doing so, they trade journalism’s ethics, standards and accountability for performance. Social media has indeed opened ways for its users to quickly receive information and news that would have otherwise remained hidden, but removing the barrier to publishing information doesn’t eliminate the need for journalistic ethics.

Recently, a wave of self-styled journalists has gone so far as to enter government offices without permission, demand explanations from employees and question officials about their attendance, identity cards and dress codes, in the name of surprise inspections, underscoring once again the need for the media industry to set the standards that distinguish journalism from ‘stunt’. While it is the duty of journalists to question and investigate whether public servants are accountable to the people they serve, journalism must follow due process. Journalists are duty-bound to conduct basic research before reporting, prepare questions in advance and arrange an interview with the relevant person. They are also supposed to verify any content before publishing it and accept legitimate criticisms from the audience.

The consequences of actions by self-appointed inspectors carrying cameras are grave. When journalism is repeatedly associated with confrontational or sensational tactics, it can erode trust between public officials and the media, affecting even journalists following professional standards. Many government employees have increasingly complained of harassment despite performing their duties properly. This makes it difficult to gain essential information from officials.

These practices invite another danger that impacts the whole profession. Governments may find justification to regulate media more aggressively if sensationalisation of content blurs the line between journalism and intimidation. In the past, there have been repeated attempts to stifle press freedom. Authorities have misused Section 47 of the Electronic Transactions Act to detain journalists and silence critics. The Social Media Bill, 2025, introduced during the premiership of KP Oli, threatened press freedom. Every unethical act conducted in the name of journalism risks emboldening those who argue that stricter controls are necessary.

A balanced approach that addresses the issue without undermining press freedom is now necessary. The Press Council has already begun monitoring the activities and content of self-styled journalists, which is a much-needed step. Some have received warnings, while in serious cases of violations, disciplinary action has begun. The onus of reclaiming journalistic standards also lies with the media industry itself. Professional organisations should speak more clearly about ethical practices in journalism. Newsrooms should invest in training journalists in ethical reporting. Digital creators who disseminate vital information on social media platforms must also adhere to the dos and don’ts of journalism. The future of journalism will not be determined by who can publish fastest, but by who can report with a greater sense of responsibility.

articles.title: Methodological mess in development research
articles.summary:
This methodological weakness of Nepal’s development research has been documented for decades. In the 1980s, researchers found that estimates of Nepali firewood use varied so wildly between studies that the numbers were simply too unreliable to say whether Himalayan forests were disappearing at all. Yet, these same numbers were treated as facts, informing a World Bank prediction that no accessible forest would remain in Nepal by 2000.

Likewise, anthropologist Judith Justice found that Nepal’s health data was produced to satisfy bureaucratic reporting requirements rather than to understand conditions on the ground. Planning documents described a Nepal that existed only on paper. Even forty years ago, research was being produced for reporting, not for understanding.

These shortcomings persist today. A large amount of research claims a ‘causal relationship’ between microfinance and women’s empowerment. These methods typically rely on before-and-after surveys. Researchers asked if the women felt empowered, and they usually responded positively because demonstrating progress provided them with continued programme access. This is a social desirability bias. The survey finds empowerment because the method is looking for empowerment. Anthropologist Katharine Rankin's ethnography shows exactly what those methods missed. Rather than asking women if they felt empowered, she asked who held authority over labour and loans within the household. She found women were targeted less for empowerment than for their reliability in repaying. As a result, repayment pressure fell on women, while investment decisions stayed with men. This shows that the method determines the finding.

In recent years, a newer method has entered Nepal’s development research landscape. Designed by Silicon Valley pioneers, human-centred design (HCD) asks researchers to build ‘empathy with users’ through short interviews, then turn the learnings into a redesigned product or intervention. HCD suffers from what is known as ‘design tourism’, where outsiders help communities build a prototype, without engaging with their deep structural power dynamics. According to communication scholar Sasha Costanza-Chock, sympathy does not redistribute authority; feeling for a community is not the same as sharing power over what gets built. Anthropologist Anke Schwittay’s research on microfinance codesign confirms this pattern. Even with genuine sympathy and good intentions, outside expertise tends to favour outsider, technological and commercial solutions over political action or indigenous practice. Nepal’s development sector needs to adopt this method with scrutiny.

Research in Nepal is overwhelmingly commissioned by donors, designed around their accountability needs, conducted by researchers selected through processes favouring prior donor relationships and interpreted for donor reporting requirements. Communities being researched have almost no role in defining the research questions, little access to findings and almost no mechanisms for challenging conclusions that might misrepresent them. According to anthropologist David Mosse, research commissioned to check whether a programme works tends to find that it does because the methodology is designed within the programme’s own framework.

Having traced these methodologies’ weakness, it is worth highlighting what rigour looks like. The Nepal Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS) and the Nepal Living Standards Survey (NLSS) show this in practice. The NDHS uses stratified probability sampling across thousands of households, standardised modules for comparison across survey rounds, and caste and ethnicity disaggregation, making inequality visible. It openly admits it relies on verbal reports, not clinical measurement, and cannot explain the causal mechanisms behind the trends it finds. The NLSS adds two further dimensions. It follows the same households across time, allowing longitudinal tracking of welfare change and spreads data collection across 12 months to capture seasonal variation. In both these cases, rigour does not mean complexity for its own sake. It means choosing methods appropriate to the questions being asked, being transparent about limitations, triangulating across multiple data sources, and designing deliberately against the social dynamics that distort findings.

Every research design should be justified against the research questions, and not chosen for convenience. A method that cannot detect a negative or an unexpected result is built to confirm whatever it was designed to find. This means being explicit about what a method can and cannot show, reflecting on likely biases, triangulating across sources before trusting a result, using mixed methods in qualitative inquiry and adopting longitudinal designs whenever observing change.

Research depends on the social context, and rigorous research helps to design against the hierarchies that shape it—through stratified data collection, working with local researchers rather than one-off enumerators, validating findings before finalising and reporting results in language communities can access and contest. Research participation is not about being a respondent, but about being part of the process that decides what the research concludes.

In Nepal’s development research, methods are largely chosen not for their ability to find evidence, but to suit the assumptions made by programmes and generate reports. Therefore, rigour is necessary because it requires designing a method that is open to new findings. That commitment requires donors willing to fund research with depth, producing inconvenient findings; institutions willing to build evidence systems communities can actually contribute to and contest; and researchers willing to design and conduct research with the possibility of learning and improvising.

articles.title: Why strong foreign policy starts at home
articles.summary:
Democratic Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, aka AOC, when asked if she will use her House seat as a platform to run for the United States presidency in 2028, said, in her usual forthright manner, that Republicans assume her ambition is ‘positional’. She implies that the assumption that she wants a platform for herself via a high position is a deeply cynical one. Actually, her ambition is much higher. What she wants is healthcare covered by the State, living wages, workers’ rights, women’s rights—changes that will last forever, not a position that is finite.

Today’s leaders in Nepal should take note. While many of us continue to believe that RSP leaders have good intentions, it is also important to keep in mind that politics is not just about position and the heady power that comes with it. It is about bringing about real change. Recently, another outspoken young woman, Sobita Gautam, the current Law Minister, was interviewed at length, where she also emphasised that politics is not about glamour; it is about putting in real work towards change.

As the RSP’s 100 days are over and we are looking towards the upcoming five years, the commitment to strengthening Nepal’s social and economic landscape is crucial to its global and geo-political situation. Our foreign policy has long been dictated by men who have wielded kompromat and used the excuse of realpolitik to fulfil their own interests. With a brand new set of more principled leaders, one hopes that kind of warped behaviour evolves into a more dignified modus operandi.

Regardless of this clean slate, without a long-term strategy of strengthening Nepal itself, our foreign policy will continue to remain feeble. Although landlocked between two behemoth superpowers, Nepal is no longer quite the squishable yam it used to be. To become an economic bridge or ‘buffer’, however, this country must hone its outward strategy with a common-sense approach of multilateralism, shrewd understanding of psychology underscored by strategic intelligence, leading to a steady action-based, long-lasting approach, executed with integrity. These aspects are essential to any sound foreign policy plan but are not nearly enough. Nepal has to be able to generate products that are worth trading so that we can finally negotiate on our own terms.

The obvious options, such as electricity production and export, are not the no-brainers they appear to be. Corruption, transmission infrastructure, procurement challenges, third-country investors and geopolitics, all play a role. The biggest elephant in the room is climate change. Adverse changes in hydrology have already affected many hydropower projects that have come online, and this trend will only continue without an urgent national and global shift in climate policy with actual provisioning, not just sham diplomacy and COP summits in problematic host countries.

Digital transformation is essential, but a thorough SWOT analysis must be conducted before extending that transformation to include exporting processing power and cloud storage. With data centres guzzling water, even with our monsoon surpluses, an investment like this without adequate research could adversely affect Nepal’s water security.

Which leads, of course, to food security. For a country that has so much agricultural promise, Nepal is now importing more food than it exports, and farmers are constantly at the mercy of fertiliser shortages in an increasingly volatile global supply. With no signs of the climate crisis easing, without serious thought towards solutions for securing our water and food supplies, Nepal, already vulnerable, will become cripplingly so. This unpreparedness will only make us ever more malleable on the global political scene, not to mention leaving us without the option to trade for power. The chance to become an agricultural export powerhouse—although decades behind due to malignant short-sightedness—is still possible with the right kind of strategic planning and infrastructure.

The weak education system contributes greatly to our economic situation. Without an outward-looking education plan that concentrates on producing a workforce with global skills, like proficiency with languages, digital familiarity, practical and out-of-the-box thinking (instead of rote skills that will swiftly be rendered obsolete by AI), Nepal will never be able to compete with a far better-trained global workforce. Our youth will go on spending more than they can afford to study abroad, or jump ship the moment they find any, even menial, opportunities abroad, weakening both our output and our communities.

Nepal needs to fully overhaul its byzantine, STEM-heavy education system to prepare for a future where original, ethical, critical and creatively trained minds will be the essential 21st-century skills. These qualities are also vital in the citizens of any country to create a national ethos that is truly liberal, even as it is civic-minded. This is the kind of training that will produce future entrepreneurs and diplomats who are profoundly engaged with Nepal’s languages, culture, domestic intricacies, strengths and weaknesses, in addition to being able to assess complex situations and sift fake news from facts—all crucial now to function at an international level.

Take Korea’s unparalleled soft power in the form of K-Pop, K-Drama and K-Beauty. These homegrown creative industries, drawing on Korea’s historical cultural strengths, have now provided that country with employment, worldwide recognition and an enormous boost in its balance of trade, all the while shoring up their resilience. Such creative industries require very little aside from ideas and intellectual property development for success. Little is imported; everything can be exported.

Investment in these domestically strong industries created an opportunity for strong export and diplomacy. Everyone knows who they are, thanks to these exports. Korea is now recognised for positive creativity instead of its endemic problems of misogyny and low birth rate. One only has to shudder through Han Kang’s The Vegetarian, the 2007 Nobel Prize-winning, searing meta-fable of domestic abuse and women-hating toxic masculinity, to see that Korean culture is not just fresh-faced glass skin, K-pop demon hunters, and happy romances.

With this new government and sincere leadership from the likes of people like Foreign Minister Sishir Khanal, whose pedigree of civil society activism is hard to match, one hopes for more space for marginalised women in diplomatic positions who will represent those who have been historically sidelined, making them the face of the country. Nepal must look inwards to strengthen its own inclusiveness and society even as it navigates the complexity of its geographical and global position by shoring up its own strengths instead of flexing wildly against forces that cannot be matched without doing our own exercises first.

Foreign policy is not about building one’s own social and political capital for personal ambition. It is not about position or glamour. It is about investing in Nepal’s culture and communities, researching and strategising on how to leverage this country’s human, social, natural, financial and physical capital for the benefit of all its 30 million people to negotiate and compete on par with the world in an increasingly globalised landscape.

articles.title: RSP promised to clean up academia. Why the sudden U-turn?
articles.summary:
The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) promised to depoliticise Nepal’s public institutions, particularly universities, by replacing existing office bearers with appointments based on transparency, merit and integrity. However, recent Vice Chancellor (VC) appointments challenge this commitment. Lower-ranked candidates under the government’s own evaluation framework were chosen over higher-ranked individuals, despite concerns regarding their professional credibility, raising serious questions about whether the selection process was genuinely merit-based. Rather than demonstrating a merit-based process, the outcome raises a broader question: Has the Government of Nepal genuinely reformed the way it selects academic leaders, or has it simply redesigned the appearance of the process?

Initially, the VC selection process seemed like a meaningful departure from the past, utilising strategic plans, interviews, a published scoring framework and online public feedback to project fairness and transparency. Collectively, these measures projected the image of a government committed to procedural fairness and institutional transparency.

Yet the credibility of any selection process depends not on the sophistication of its procedures but on the consistency between those procedures and the outcome. Transparency in a democratic government does not require that the highest-scoring candidate always be selected. It does require that when governments depart from the framework they establish, they clearly explain why. Without that explanation, the public is left unable to understand whether the decision reflected legitimate judgment or political influence.

The process itself also raises questions that deserve careful public consideration. If the published scoring model was not intended to influence the final decision substantially, what purpose did it serve? If the government intended to demonstrate that political considerations would no longer shape university appointments, why have the outcomes renewed debate about political influence rather than academic leadership?

Equally important is the composition of the selection process itself. What qualifications were used in selecting the expert panel? Were these individuals the country’s foremost authorities in higher education governance and university administration, and on what basis were they entrusted with evaluating candidates who, in several cases, possessed decades of senior academic and administrative experience?

Finally, if stakeholder perspectives were considered valuable, why was consultation conducted through an unrestricted online survey rather than directed toward those with a direct institutional stake in the university, its faculty, researchers, students, alumni and administrative staff?

Public engagement is an important component of democratic governance, but participation strengthens institutional legitimacy only when it is meaningful. An unrestricted online survey may create the appearance of participation, but it does little to strengthen confidence in decisions involving specialised leadership.

The disappointment over the university appointments is significant because RSP had promised transparency, systems over personalities, and institutions over patronage. Whether the final appointments are justified or not, the process has raised many questions on whether RSP’s promises are being reflected in institutional practice.

The consequences extend well beyond a single appointment. It is about whether Nepal is building institutions that reward intellectual integrity, administrative competence and public service, or institutions that merely perform those values while operating according to a different set of rules. When governments invite accomplished academics to prepare detailed strategic proposals, participate in extensive interviews and compete under published evaluation criteria, they create a reasonable expectation that merit will play a central role in determining the outcome. If that expectation is later undermined, the damage is institutional rather than personal. Such a facade of transparency erodes public confidence more deeply than the opaque systems it was intended to replace.

This is perhaps the greatest cost of performative transparency. Every time governments ask professionals to devote their expertise to elaborate competitions without demonstrating that the published rules genuinely matter, the result is the gradual erosion of intellectual capital. Talented individuals begin to conclude that intellectual preparation, administrative experience and academic achievement are secondary to politics.

Nepal frequently speaks of reversing brain drain, strengthening higher education and building knowledge-based institutions. Those ambitions cannot be realised without public trust. Talented people do not commit their lives to institutions they believe are indifferent to merit. Nepal cannot simultaneously lament the departure of its brightest minds while creating appointment processes that leave many questioning whether professional excellence is genuinely rewarded. Intellectual integrity is sustained not through speeches about reform, but through institutions that consistently demonstrate, through their decisions, that merit matters.

Perhaps the deepest concern is that this culture extends beyond any one government or political party. It points to institutional structures that repeatedly reward loyalty over competence and discourage those who seek to serve through expertise and public service. It is the same old theatrics and game of power and hunger, just a change in the people. Whether it is the old guard or the new wave, the rot is not in the people at the top, but in the soil of the system itself.

Good people can never do good because the system is designed to suffocate them. Those who participated in good faith invested significant time, effort and preparation, believing that integrity, merit and genuine competition still held value within Nepal’s public institutions. If the outcome was ultimately shaped by considerations that outweighed the published process, then those efforts served little purpose beyond legitimising a decision whose reasoning remains unexplained.

Merit-based selection cannot coexist with opaque decision-making. This erodes hope for citizens who value public service, creating the perception that merit is secondary to political calculations. Ultimately, it discourages the principled, qualified individuals Nepal’s public institutions need to attract.

The single request to public leaders is simply this: Be honest.

Governments come and go. Political parties rise and fall. But institutions endure. Their legitimacy depends not on the promises leaders make, but on whether their actions consistently reflect the principles they proclaim.

If Nepal truly seeks to build world-class universities capable of retaining talented scholars, inspiring future generations and reversing the country’s persistent brain drain, then merit cannot simply be celebrated in speeches. It must be visible in the decisions that matter most. Because when the appearance of transparency becomes more important than transparency itself, it is not only merit that dies in the dark. Public trust dies with it.

articles.title: Documentary film review: The revolution that took their childhoods
articles.summary:
Robot Koenig’s ‘Returned: Child Soldiers of Nepal’s Maoist Army’ is a 2008 documentary film which follows the lives of a few of the many thousand child soldiers who have returned home after the end of the Nepali Civil War.

The documentary features the to-be-expected cast of journalists, scholars, experts, politicians and diplomats, but at its core are the child soldiers – their motivations in joining the war, their experience of the conflict and their difficult reintegration and return home.

The audience is first introduced to Ashish, who shares that he joined the war to fight for every Nepali’s right to food, clothing and shelter. As Ashish continues to share his story, however, it becomes evident his joining the ‘People’s Liberation Army’ was not entirely voluntary. The Maoist had come to Ashish’s village school to take them to a ‘cultural programme'. The students were to be returned home the next day.

Ashish’s narration of the exact events is unclear, but it would appear the Maoist leaders of the cultural programme had taken off with the children, including Ashish, who was 15 at the time.

Following the end of the war, Ashish returns home. He shares that he has wanted to continue his education, something he seems to have been unable to do, even after the war, owing to his family’s financial situation. Ashish’s father finds his son to have become more aloof. “He does not tell me anything. We don’t really talk," he says.

Some soldiers reflect back on their experiences proudly. Many from oppressed castes, soldiers enjoyed a certain power and dignity they were sure to be denied otherwise.

One young soldier, speaking anonymously, shares that he thought he kept his village peaceful during the conflict by shutting down card games, burning playing cards and silencing those he had felt disrespected by in the past. The soldier’s words feel misplaced. Here is a child maybe of 13 or 14, who ought to be in school reading poetry with his peers; in effect, it would appear, in charge of his village, dispensing justice as he sees fit.

Other soldiers seem to have joined the Maoists out of sheer childlike fascination. One young girl speaks of the Maoists with admiration. ‘These people live in the jungle. They can even take on the Royal Army with all their guns,” she says.

Preeti, who joined the People’s Liberation Army at 14, alleges then Royal Army raped women, looted houses, stole things and beat villagers. And that it was only after the village came under Maoist control that these activities stopped.

One child soldier, Ramesh, is motivated to join the guerrillas after the Royal Army took their father from their home, beat him and finally shot him to death at 4 a.m. one morning. His sister, however, stays back.

The documentary does a fine job showcasing the varying motivations and circumstances that led to the child soldiers joining the army.

No two stories are exactly the same, yet they share similar undercurrents. The lack of opportunities in the countryside, the inhumane realities of caste and gender, and the brutality brought on by the conflict, one finds, played a major role in convincing the children to pick up arms.

Similarly, no two returns are the same. And yet they too share similar undercurrents. The returned children are faced with a village and, on many occasions, a family which does not want them back. The children return from their fantastical lives as revolutionaries to a countryside which largely remains unchanged.

The women who fled their backward communities find themselves trying to reintegrate into those very same communities where they are now labelled ‘impure’ for having mingled with boys in the jungle.

One young girl shares the heartbreaking fate that was awaiting her upon her return. Upon her return, she is married off to an older man. She is only 14 at the time. When her new family finds out she used to be a Maoist soldier, they refuse to accept her. Beaten by her husband and abused by her in-laws, she tries, unsuccessfully, to hang herself.

Past the incessant use of Nepali folk music, Koenig’s film confronts viewers with uncomfortable questions, many of which have been lost in the public discourse in the two decades following the conflict.

Children, in the thousands, were plunged into a conflict they did not fully understand. And at the end of ten years, they found themselves just as poor, living in communities sometimes just as backwards and faced with additional discrimination and the reality of their lost childhoods.

The children in the documentary are largely uneducated and untrained in any income-generating trades.

In light of the Supreme Court’s recent decision on Lenin Bista’s writ, the film provides vivid images and stories of the conflict helpful in beginning to understand the 10 years of war, its ramifications, where we have come from, and where it remains for us to go.

Returned: Child Soldiers of Nepal's Maoist Army

Publisher: University of Cambridge

Direction, Production and Copyright: Robert Koenig

Duration: 60 minutes

Available on YouTube

articles.title: Fiction: Palpali dhakatopi pasal
articles.summary:
The hills of Tansen had always seemed eternal. From the stone-paved lanes of the old bazaar to the terraced fields that wrapped themselves around the slopes like green shawls, life moved slowly in the Palpa bazaar. The mornings smelled of wood smoke and fresh tea filled the air. Temple bells echoed through the surrounding hills. And in a small house overlooking the winding road, Mitralal and Saraswati had spent nearly five decades building a life together.

Their only son, Gokarna, owned a tiny shop named Palpali Dhakatopi Pasal in the main street of Tansen Bazaar.

The shop was not much to look at. Its wooden signboard had faded with age. Though the shop was small, it had a nice collection of all brands of Dhakatopis. The shop always filled Mitralal with pride and a sense of success. He neatly displayed traditional Dhakatopis on a wooden rack, displaying intricate patterns woven by skilled hands. Tourists bought them as souvenirs. Local men wore them during festivals and weddings. Government officials often stopped by to purchase one before important ceremonies.

To Gokarna, the shop was his grandfather's legacy. It was the thread that connected his family to generations of Nepali tradition. Every morning, Mitralal would worship the goddess Laxmi before meeting his customers.

But one winter, Mitralal's health began to fail rapidly. At first it was simple fatigue. Then came breathing difficulties. His legs weakened, and his memory sometimes wandered. Doctors in Tansen prescribed medicines and advised rest.

One cold morning, as mist rolled across the hills, Mitralal closed his eyes and never opened them again.

The funeral rites were performed beside the river. The smoke from the cremation pyre rose toward the pale sky. Saraswati stood silently. Her hands trembled. For fifty years she had shared every joy and hardship with her husband. Now the house felt unbearably empty. For many days at night she still reached toward his side of the bed before remembering he was gone.

Gokarna suffered too. He buried himself in work, opening the shop before sunrise and closing it long after dark.

Several months later, tragedy struck again. It happened on a stormy evening. A short circuit sparked inside the shop, and within minutes flames spread through the dry wooden shelves. By the time neighbours noticed, the fire had already engulfed the shop.

The bright Dhakatopis that had symbolised generations of labour burned like paper lanterns.

People formed lines carrying buckets of water. Someone called the fire brigade. But nothing could save the shop. When dawn arrived, only blackened beams remained. Gokarna stood in the ashes, staring silently.

The family had lost everything. Their only source of income was gone. For weeks Gokarna searched for solutions. He borrowed money from relatives and met lenders. But the money he had collected was not enough to rebuild their business once again. Finally, with tears in his eyes, he sat beside his mother.

"I have decided to go abroad."

Saraswati's heart sank. She looked at her son inquisitively.

“Ama, the money is not enough to begin the shop again. That’s why I want to go to Dubai”, said Gokarna.

"Dubai." Saraswati was surprised at her son’s decision.

"I found work in a garment factory. If I stay there for a few years, I can repay the loans and rebuild the shop once again." Saraswati looked at her son's face silently and nodded her head in affirmation.

"How long will you stay abroad?" she asked.

"Not long, Ama. As soon as I earn enough to rebuild our shop, I will return," said Gokarna and held his mother’s hands.

"I promise, Ama. One day we'll open a Dhakatopi shop that will be better than the previous one."

A few months later, he left. The bus carried him away through the winding roads. Saraswati stood atop a large boulder watching until the bus disappeared beyond the hills. Then she returned home alone.

The years that followed moved strangely. Days felt endless. Months disappeared quickly. Gokarna called whenever possible but sent money regularly.

Saraswati treasured every memory of her son. Yet loneliness slowly settled into the house like dust. Over the years, her eyesight began to deteriorate. At first she struggled to thread a needle.

Then faces became blurry. Eventually she could barely recognise visitors standing in front of her.

Doctors said her vision was failing badly. She had minor surgery on her eyes, but that too did not work. Her daily life activities became much more difficult. One evening, after a particularly difficult day, she spoke to Gokarna over the phone.

"My son, I don't know how much longer my eyes will last. At this moment, I don't need money anymore. I only want you to stay with me." Gokarna promised his mother to come home in a few days.

Then one midnight, as rain tapped softly against the roof, someone knocked on the door. Saraswati awoke immediately. Her heart raced.

"Who is it?"

"Ama." The voice was familiar. Her happiness knew no bounds.

"Yes." She hurried toward the door. The moment she touched his face, tears streamed down her cheeks.

"My son..."

Gokarna embraced his mother gently.

For the first time in years, the house felt alive again. That night they talked until dawn. Gokarna explained to his mother that he would be busy in the daytime arranging a new shop and meeting suppliers. He could not stay long during the day but return home at night. Saraswati did not mind. For her, the presence of her son was enough.

This became a daily routine for Gokarna. He would arrive home daily at midnight and bring delicious food with him. Both ate food together and talked and laughed late into the night.

For Saraswati, happiness returned. Neighbours, however, grew concerned. During the daytime she was almost always alone. No one saw Gokarna in the marketplace. No one saw him rebuilding a shop. Yet every time they asked, Saraswati smiled.

"During the daytime, my son is very busy at his shop, but he comes home daily at midnight”. At this, the neighbours exchanged worried glances but spoke nothing.

Then one afternoon, a government official arrived carrying a sealed envelope. He introduced himself politely and sat beside Saraswati.

"Ama, a body was found near Pokhara several months ago. It belonged to a young man. The face was badly damaged; that’s why the police could not identify him." The official hesitated but continued.

"We found documents suggesting he could be your son, Gokarna. So, the authority here in Palpa wants you to visit Pokhara for the DNA testing."

But Saraswati blasted in anger and asked the man to get out of her house immediately.

“My son is with me. At this very moment, he is at his shop. Don’t you know our shop? It is the Palpali Dhakatopi Pasal, one of the oldest shops in Palpa. Every evening, my son returns home, and we always have dinner together. Yet you claim that the police found my son’s body several months ago. How could that possibly be true when he is living with me? He spends his days busy at the shop, and every night he comes home with food. We sit down together and have dinner. So how can you say that my son died months ago?”

Looking at Saraswati, fuming with anger, the official man was scared and immediately left. However, the neighbours remained confused. After leaving for Dubai, the neighbours had never seen Gokarna in Tansen. The Palpali Dhakatopi Pasal was never rebuilt.

That night, some curious neighbours decided to wait until midnight to see Gokarna. They stood near the door patiently. It was midnight when Saraswati opened the door with a broad smile across her face and closed the door.

The neighbours hurried to the nearest window, eager to catch a glimpse of Gokarna. However, a thick curtain drawn across the window and the faint glow of a dim lamp prevented them from seeing clearly inside the room. Moments later, they heard the clinking of spoons against plates, followed by Saraswati's cheerful voice praising the delicious food. She continued talking for hours, as though engaged in a lively conversation, and now and then her laughter rang through the quiet night. The neighbours stood motionless, gripped by a mixture of fear and bewilderment. Unable to make sense of what they had witnessed, they slowly returned to their respective homes, their minds filled with confusion and unanswered questions.

Years have passed, but still people in Tansen Bazaar say that at midnight one can hear Saraswati talking with her son Gokarna.

articles.title: EXHIBIT REVIEW: On recollections of homeland
articles.summary:
